pages.text: Here is lesson 3's turning arm on a circle, pointing right to start. Lift a copy of it off as a bendy rod, exactly one radius long, and lay it round the edge from where the arm starts. Turn the arm anticlockwise until it meets the rod's far end. The angle it has opened at the centre is one [[radian]], because its [[arc]], the stretch of edge between the two arms, is one radius long. Two rods laid end to end make 2 radians. Drag the tip of the arm, or the size handle on the edge.

pages.alt: A circle of radius 2 metres drawn to scale, with an arc 4 metres long between two arms. The angle at the centre is 2 radians: the arc holds two radius-lengths.
pages.name: An arc of 4 m
pages.task: An arc of 4 m sits on a circle of radius 2 m. What angle does it make at the centre?
pages.why: Count the arc in radius-lengths. Each radius is 2 m, so the 4 m arc holds `4 ÷ 2 = 2` of them, and the angle is 2 radians. Arc ÷ radius gives the angle.

However big the circle, the count of rods stays the same.

pages.text: Hold the arm at 1 radian and make the circle bigger. The radius grows, so the rod grows with it. A bigger circle is the same shape drawn at a bigger scale, as lesson 1's triangles were, so the arc between the same two arms grows in step. Rod and arc grow together, so the count stays at 1.00 on every circle. That is why the angle in radians can be worked out as [[arc ÷ radius]]. Drag the size handle on the edge.

pages.alt: Two circles drawn to scale: above, radius 1 metre with an arc of 1 metre; below, radius 3 metres with an arc of 3 metres. Each angle at the centre is 1 radian.
pages.name: Two circles
options: The big circle's, 3 times as big
pages.task: A circle of radius 1 m has an arc of 1 m. A circle of radius 3 m has an arc of 3 m. Which angle at the centre is bigger?
pages.why: Each arc is exactly one radius long, `1 m ÷ 1 m = 1` and `3 m ÷ 3 m = 1`, so each angle is 1 radian. The big circle's arc is longer only because its radius is longer too.

pages.alt: A circle with lesson 3's arm turned anticlockwise 6.28 radians, 360.0 degrees, from where it started, pointing right. A bendy rod one radius long is laid round the edge from the start: 6 whole radius-lengths and 0.28 of another. A size handle on the edge grows or shrinks the circle. A dashed line marks the half turn, and one rod's slice of the circle, 57.3 degrees, is shaded.
pages.name: All the way round
pages.text: Now lay the rod all the way round. The edge is the circumference, `2πr`, so it holds `2πr ÷ r = 2π` rods, six whole rods and 0.28 of a seventh. A full turn is 360°, so `360° = 2π radians`. Halfway round the count is 3.14, which is π, so `180° = π radians`. One rod's slice is `180° ÷ π`, about 57.3°, a little under a sixth of the circle, not the whole circle. Drag the tip of the arm.

pages.alt: A circle with two arms at a right angle, a quarter of a turn, the arc between them marked on the edge. Round it lie one whole rod and 0.57 of another: 1.57 radius-lengths.
pages.name: A quarter turn
pages.task: How many radius-lengths fit round a quarter of the circle?
pages.why: A full turn holds 2π rods, about 6.28, so a quarter holds `6.28 ÷ 4 = 1.57`. That is π ÷ 2, one whole rod and a little over half another. One radian is only 57.3°, short of the quarter's 90°.

pages.alt: One circle with arms from the start, pointing right. Two thin arms mark the conversions: 60 degrees, 1.047 radians, and 2 radians, 114.6 degrees. A solid arm turned 10 degrees, a small turn. A dashed arm turned 10 radians, whose path wraps 1.59 times round outside the edge and stops at 213.0 degrees, left of the centre and below it. Rows give the conversions and the two cosines.
pages.name: Degrees and radians
pages.text: Here are the two conversions at work. `60° × π ÷ 180 = 1.047` radians, and 2 radians is `2 × 180 ÷ π = 114.6°`. Exam courses such as SQA Higher take an angle with no degree sign, as in `cos 10`, to be in radians, so the calculator must be in radian mode. The two can be far apart. 10° is a small turn, but 10 radians wraps 1.59 times round and stops at 213.0°, left of the centre and below it. The cosine is the arm's shadow across, as in lesson 3, so there it is negative: `cos 10 = −0.839`, against 0.985 for 10°.

pages.why: To turn degrees into radians, multiply by `π ÷ 180`. So `45 × π ÷ 180 = 0.785`, which is π ÷ 4, half the quarter turn's 1.57. A check on size: a radian is about 57.3°, so the degree figure is about 57.3 times the radian figure.

pages.alt: A winch drum of radius 0.2 metres, turned 2.5 radians. The wire it has wound on lies round its edge, 2 whole radius-lengths and 0.5 of another, and the hook below has risen 0.5 metres from where it started.
pages.name: Arc length
pages.text: Each radian of angle holds one radius of edge, so θ radians on a circle of radius `r` hold an arc `s = rθ`, with θ in radians. Say a winch drum of radius 0.2 m turns through 2.5 radians. The wire it winds on lies round its edge, two whole radius-lengths and half of another, so `s = 0.2 × 2.5 = 0.5` m, and the hook rises 0.5 m. Drag the arm on the drum to turn it.

pages.name: The arc at 60°

pages.task: A circle has a radius of 0.5 m. How long is the arc between two arms 60° apart?
pages.why: `s = rθ` needs θ in radians. First `60° × π ÷ 180 = 1.047` radians, then `s = 0.5 × 1.047 = 0.524` m. A check: the whole edge is `2π × 0.5 = 3.14` m, and 60° is a sixth of a turn, so the arc is a sixth of 3.14 m.

pages.alt: The end of a shaft turning at 400 rev/min. Its arm has turned 6.28 radians, the rod laid behind it: 6 whole radius-lengths and 0.28 of another. Rows give its angular speed and power.
pages.name: Turning speed
pages.text: Turning speed is counted the same way. Bird's engineering textbook works through a ship's drive shaft turning at 400 rev/min, 400 turns a minute. Each turn is 2π radians, so it turns through `400 × 2π` radians a minute, and a minute is 60 seconds. Its [[angular speed]], ω, the Greek letter omega, is `400 × 2π ÷ 60 = 41.9` radians a second, written rad/s. A shaft's power is its torque times ω, so with Bird's torque of 400 kN m it delivers 16.76 MW.

pages.task: An angle is given as 0.5, with no degree sign. What is its sine?
pages.why: No degree sign means radians, so the calculator goes in radian mode, and `sin 0.5 = 0.479`. On the picture the arm's tip has travelled 0.5 of a radius round the edge, and its height, the sine, is a little less than that arc.

pages.task: A motor shaft turns at 1,500 rev/min. What is its angular speed, in rad/s?
pages.why: Each turn is 2π radians, so 1,500 turns a minute is `1,500 × 2π = 9,425` radians a minute. A minute is 60 seconds, so `ω = 9,425 ÷ 60 = 157.1` rad/s.

pages.task: A sheave, a grooved wheel, of radius 0.25 m makes 3 full turns. How much rope passes over it?
pages.why: Each full turn is 2π radians, so 3 turns are `3 × 2π = 6π` radians. With θ in radians, `s = rθ = 0.25 × 6π = 4.71` m, three times the sheave's edge.
